title: Distance to Poles: How Far to 90°N and 90°S
description: Measure your great-circle distance to the geographic North and South Poles with Distance to Poles — miles and km from any place on Earth. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, New York sits approx. 3,405 miles (5,481 km) from the North Pole and approx. 9,031 miles (14,535 km) from the South Pole — polar distance is just latitude, measured.
quick_answer: Distance to Poles measures the great-circle distance from any place to the North Pole and South Pole. Because the poles sit at the ends of the Earth's axis, the answer is latitude geometry: your distance to the nearer pole depends only on how far your latitude is from ninety degrees.
steps_intro: Two fixed points, every place on Earth, one clean piece of geometry:

body.t: The poles make latitude tangible: a class can watch the North Pole distance shrink by about 69 miles for every degree travelled north, because that is literally what a degree of latitude is.
Polar-night and aurora questions are latitude questions. This measure frames how 'polar' a place like Tromsø or Fairbanks really is before the detailed planning starts.
Which is closer to a pole, Reykjavík or Anchorage? The argument ends here, with a method anyone can rerun — the
tool then settles the city-to-city version.
Pair this with the antipode tools to explore the planet's extremes: farthest from the pole, farthest from your own antipode, closest to the axis ends.

New York (40.7128° N): to the North Pole approx. 5,480.5 km (3,405.4 mi) — that is (90 − 40.7128) = 49.2872° of arc; to the South Pole approx. 14,534.6 km (9,031.4 mi). The two always sum to the half-circumference, approx. 20,015 km.

London (51.5072° N) to the South Pole: approx. 15,734.9 km (9,777.2 mi) — near the maximum any northern city can be from the far pole. Its North Pole distance is correspondingly shorter, which the tool shows side by side.

popular_table.title: The latitude ladder
popular_table.intro: Distance to the North Pole depends only on latitude: it is (90° − latitude) of arc on the site model. Read your latitude, read your polar distance.
popular_table.note: Figures are (90 ∓ latitude) × 111.195 km per degree on the mean sphere, rounded — the tool computes the exact haversine for your point.

faq: The poles are the axis endpoints: every meridian runs into them. Moving east or west changes your longitude but not your angular distance to the pole, so the great-circle distance to a pole is set by latitude alone.
The geographic North Pole is 90° N (longitude is undefined there — every direction from it is south) and the South Pole is 90° S, where every direction is north. The tool uses those fixed points.
Is the reverse bearing from the pole meaningful?
No — and the tool will not pretend otherwise. From the North Pole every heading is 180° (south). Bearings to the pole are clean; bearings from it are a special case the geometry honestly refuses.
Geographic — the axis endpoints. The magnetic poles wander (the north magnetic pole is in the Canadian Arctic) and belong to the Magnetic Declination tool's subject, not this one.
Why do the two distances sum to about 20,015 km?
Because pole-to-pole along any meridian is a half circumference: π × 6,371.0088 km ≈ 20,015 km. Your two distances are the two pieces of that arc through your meridian.
Can a place be equidistant from both poles?
Yes — everywhere on the equator, at approx. 10,007.6 km (6,218.4 mi) from each. It is the only parallel with that property.
Does the tool work in the southern hemisphere?
Yes — the ladder simply reads the other way: southern places are close to the South Pole and far from the North.
